cards.title: Constant-factor treewidth preservation by subcubic subgraphs
cards.formal:
Does there exist a real constant \(C\ge1\) such that every finite nonempty simple undirected graph \(G\) has a nonempty subgraph \(H\) satisfying
\[
\Delta(H)\le3
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{tw}(H)\ge\frac{\operatorname{tw}(G)}{C}?
\]
Here \(H\) is obtained solely by deleting vertices and edges of \(G\), \(\Delta\) is maximum degree, and \(\operatorname{tw}\) is treewidth. The same constant \(C\) must work for all graphs.
cards.definitions:
A finite nonempty simple undirected graph \(F=(V(F),E(F))\) has a finite nonempty vertex set and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with no parallel edges. An ordinary subgraph \(H\) of \(G\) has \(\varnothing\ne V(H)\subseteq V(G)\) and
\[
E(H)\subseteq E(G)\cap\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V(H),\ u\ne v\}.
\]
Vertices and edges may be deleted; edges cannot be contracted, and new vertices or edges cannot be introduced. The subgraph need not be induced, connected or spanning. The degree of \(v\in V(H)\) is the number of its neighbors in \(H\), and \(\Delta(H)\) is the largest such degree. A graph with maximum degree at most three is called subcubic; its vertices need not all have degree three.

A tree decomposition of a nonempty graph \(F\) consists of a finite nonempty tree \(T\) and vertex bags \(B_t\subseteq V(F)\) for its nodes \(t\), satisfying three conditions: every vertex of \(F\) belongs to some bag; both endpoints of every edge belong to a common bag; and for each vertex \(v\), the nodes \(t\) with \(v\in B_t\) induce a nonempty connected subtree of \(T\). The width is \(\max_{t\in V(T)}|B_t|-1\), and \(\operatorname{tw}(F)\) is the minimum width over all tree decompositions of \(F\). In particular, a nonempty edgeless graph has treewidth zero.

The constant \(C\) is independent of the graph, its number of vertices, its maximum degree and its treewidth. The input graph is otherwise unrestricted. There is no upper bound on the size of \(H\) in terms of \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\), and no algorithm, running-time bound or randomness requirement is part of this existential statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed proposition, or a complete Lean proof of its logical negation. The positive direction must supply one finite universal constant and prove the existence of a permitted subgraph for every graph. The negation is that, for every real \(C\ge1\), there is a finite nonempty simple undirected graph \(G\) such that every nonempty ordinary subgraph \(H\) with \(\Delta(H)\le3\) satisfies \(\operatorname{tw}(H)<\operatorname{tw}(G)/C\). A factor growing with the input, a result restricted to a special graph class, or a conditional theorem alone does not settle the target.
cards.why: Treewidth is a central measure of graph structure. This question asks whether a graph can always retain a constant fraction of that structure after every vertex degree is reduced to at most three, regardless of its original degrees or density.

importance.reason: A structural sparsification principle for a central graph parameter; the gap concerns universal preservation rather than a particular construction.

progress.text: Theorem 1.1 gives a subcubic topological minor of treewidth \(\Omega(k/\operatorname{polylog}k)\) and \(O(k^4)\) vertices, and hence the corresponding ordinary-subgraph existence guarantee without that vertex bound.
Chekuri’s primary-author answer states the subcubic polylogarithmic guarantee, and his accompanying comment calls constant-degree constant-factor preservation an open problem.

Bonnet’s arXiv version 1 recalls the general polylogarithmic-loss subcubic theorem and proves a different sparsification result for induced subgraphs of graphs excluding a fixed complete bipartite subgraph.
Sparse Induced Subgraphs of Large Treewidth appears in Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 173, pages 184–203; the publisher’s introduction also recalls the Chekuri–Chuzhoy subcubic guarantee.

context_blocks.text: Amarilli’s question list explicitly asks for a subcubic ordinary subgraph preserving a constant fraction of treewidth. This card selects its treewidth question; the separately listed pathwidth question is not included.

Chekuri and Chuzhoy prove a general guarantee of \(\Omega(k/\operatorname{polylog}k)\) retained treewidth, where \(k\) is the original treewidth and \(\operatorname{polylog}k\) denotes a fixed power of its logarithm in an asymptotic bound. Their theorem produces a subcubic topological minor: a graph whose edges can be replaced by internally vertex-disjoint paths to obtain an ordinary subgraph of the input. The corresponding subdivision supplies the ordinary subgraph guarantee with the same polylogarithmic loss.

Theorem 1.1 also bounds the number of vertices of the topological minor by \(O(k^4)\). That bound applies before its edges are expanded to paths and is not a bound on the number of vertices of the resulting ordinary subgraph. The card imposes neither this size condition nor the randomized polynomial-time construction provided by the theorem.

Chekuri explicitly described constant-factor preservation with constant maximum degree as open in his August 2017 answer and comment. Amarilli’s follow-up distinguishes the ordinary-subgraph question from the stronger requirement that the compressed sparsifier have size polynomial in the treewidth.

Bonnet’s later paper studies induced subgraphs, which retain every input edge between their selected vertices. It excludes sufficiently large complete bipartite subgraphs from the input and bounds the output’s average degree rather than its maximum degree. Its guarantee is not constant-factor treewidth preservation for unrestricted inputs; its introduction still cites the polylogarithmic-loss subcubic theorem.

sentences: The question asks whether every finite graph contains a subgraph with maximum degree at most three and treewidth within a universal constant factor of the original.
The subgraph may delete vertices and edges but cannot contract edges or add new ones.
It need not be induced, connected or spanning, and no size or construction-time bound is required.
The checked general theorem preserves treewidth up to a polylogarithmic factor, leaving the constant-factor target unresolved in the cited sources.
A positive answer would show that bounded-degree subgraphs universally preserve the scale of treewidth, even in graphs of high degree.

checked_sources: Read the full canonical TCS-7245 card and applied the repository rules already read in this session. Read the actual Chekuri–Chuzhoy SODA PDF, especially page 2: topological-minor definition; Theorem 1.1, with randomized polynomial construction, polylogarithmic treewidth loss, degree three and O(k^4) compressed vertices; Conjecture 1.1 concerning O(k^2) compressed vertices; and the separate subsequent constant-factor question with polynomial size. The ordinary-subgraph corollary follows using the stated subdivision witness; a size bound for that expanded witness was not inferred.

Downloaded and read the actual full preprint arXiv:1410.1016v1, submitted 4 October 2014, PDF pages 2–3. Theorem 1.1 agrees with the conference statement. The size conjecture is numbered 1.2 in this version, unlike 1.1 in the conference PDF. The following constant-factor paragraph additionally asks for polynomial compressed size, so it is not silently identified with the weaker no-size target.

Read the primary author discussion on TCS Stack Exchange: Amarilli’s question of 28 August 2017, Chekuri’s answer and open-problem comment of 29 August, and Amarilli’s clarification of 30 August that his ordinary-subgraph question does not require a polynomial-size compressed representation. Read the current dedicated Amarilli question-list entry; it explicitly asks for degree at most three and records last seen open in 2017. The access date is not treated as a new dated research claim of openness.

Read Bonnet’s actual author-hosted manuscript and arXiv:2405.13797v1, posted 22 May 2024, Introduction pages 1–4. Theorem 1 on page 2 says that for all natural t,w and positive epsilon there is W(t,w,epsilon) such that a graph of treewidth at least W with no K_{t,t} subgraph has a 2-connected induced n-vertex subgraph of treewidth at least w and at most (1+epsilon)n edges. These quantifiers, input restriction and average-degree guarantee do not settle constant-factor subcubic preservation. The stronger description of the output is Theorem 5 on page 4. Checked the publisher metadata, abstract and introduction for DOI 10.1016/j.jctb.2025.03.002, JCTB 173 (July 2025), 184–203; the final journal PDF was not independently read.

As an additional later-source check, read the author-hosted revised Treewidth is Polynomial in Maximum Degree on Weakly Sparse Graphs Excluding a Planar Induced Minor, by Bonnet, Hodor, Korhonen and Masařík: its abstract and corrected-scope warning on page 1, and Section 3, Theorem 6, page 4. Theorem 6 again invokes the Chekuri–Chuzhoy subcubic polylogarithmic bound. The first-version gap warning concerns a different induced-minor theorem; neither it nor its correction gives a resolution here. No exact publication date for this mutable author PDF was inferred from the search engine date.

Performed bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 combining subcubic or degree-three subgraphs, treewidth sparsifiers, constant-factor or linear preservation, and 2024–2026 dates. No matching positive theorem or counterexample was found. The 2025 NP-completeness result for treewidth of cubic graphs is computational rather than this existence question; the 2026 results found about induced minors, special graph classes or subcubic running times likewise do not establish the target. This is a bounded source review, not an exhaustive current-openness certificate or a full proof audit.
quality_review.scope: Checked target, definitions, quantifiers, answer criterion, context, significance and dated source claims. Bounded later-work checks do not independently certify every cited proof.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
